summary: Specifies OSPF extensions that use Link-Local Signaling to let a router tell its neighbors what metric to use for the link toward it. This lets a router influence how much traffic comes its way, which helps in cases like maintenance. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A road crew can put up a sign saying treat this road as longer than it is. Then drivers choose other roads while work happens.

questions: how to steer traffic away from an ospf router
how does ospf reverse metric o flag work
how to drain an ospf link for maintenance
subtitle: Lets an OSPF router tell its neighbor what metric to use for the link back toward it.

tldr.problem: In OSPF each router sets the metric only for traffic it sends out a link, so a router cannot influence the traffic arriving at it on that link.
tldr.mechanism: The router puts a Reverse Metric TLV (or Reverse TE Metric TLV) in the Link-Local Signaling block of its Hello packets, and the neighbor uses that value as its own metric for the link.
tldr.outcome: Operators can drain a link for maintenance or shift load adaptively from one router, and keep metrics symmetric. Both sending and accepting must be explicitly enabled.

today: RFC 9339 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2022, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It draws on the same idea used for IS-IS in RFC 8500.

sections.title: The One-Sided Metric Problem
sections.content:
A router running OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 originates a Router-LSA describing its links, including a metric, the "cost" of reaching the neighbor over that link. For two routers R1 and R2 on a link, R1 configures the metric in the direction R1 to R2, and R2 configures it in the other direction. So R1's configuration affects the traffic it sends toward R2 but not what it receives from R2.

The reverse metric (RM) fixes that. When R1 signals its RM on the link, R2 advertises that value as its metric to R1 in its Router-LSA instead of its locally configured one. Every other router then computes paths using it, which may shift traffic the way R1 wanted.

The signaling is built on OSPF Link-Local Signaling (LLS) from RFC 5613.
sections.eli5: Normally each end of a road decides how long the road looks to its own drivers. Reverse metric lets one end say how long the road should look to the drivers at the other end.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC describes two use cases on a dual hub-and-spoke topology, where routers R1 through RN connect to both AGGR1 and AGGR2, which aggregate traffic toward a core network. It says the mechanism is generic and not limited to these cases.

Link maintenance. Before work on a link, operators raise the OSPF metric to the maximum on both routers on that link so traffic moves to alternate paths. Doing this on two devices in a coordinated way is hard, especially on routers with several hundred interfaces, or when customer edge routers are not managed by the provider. With RM, the operator puts the link in "maintenance mode" on one router. It advertises the maximum metric and signals its neighbor to do the same. Turning maintenance mode off reverts both.

Adaptive metric signaling. If AGGR1 loses capacity toward the core, changing its own metrics would only affect traffic coming from the core. It can instead signal an incremental RM to some or all of R1 through RN. They add it to their provisioned metric toward AGGR1, so the path via AGGR2 becomes better. The RM mechanism may be similarly applied between spine and leaf nodes in a Clos network.
sections.eli5: If a road needs repairs, one crew puts up one sign and both directions avoid it. If one highway gets crowded, it can ask side roads to look a bit longer so cars go elsewhere.

sections.title: The Hello-Based Design
sections.content:
A router signals RM by including a Reverse Metric TLV in its OSPF Hello packets. This scopes the signal to one specific link. The router keeps including the TLV for as long as it needs its neighbor to use that value.

The mechanism applies only to point-to-point (P2P), point-to-multipoint (P2MP) and hybrid broadcast-P2MP links. It does not apply to broadcast or NBMA links, where the same goal is reached for OSPFv2 with the OSPF Two-Part Metric (RFC 8042). An OSPFv3 solution for those link types is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The router keeps repeating its request in its regular hello message to its neighbor, only on the road in question.

sections.title: The Reverse Metric and Reverse TE Metric TLVs
sections.content:
The Reverse Metric TLV has Type 19 and Length 4 octets. It carries an MTID (the multi-topology identifier of the link), a one-octet Flags field and a two-octet unsigned Reverse Metric that replaces, or is added to, the provisioned link metric.

Two flags are defined, and the rest MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception. H (0x1) means the neighbor should use the value only if it is higher than its provisioned metric. O (0x2) means the value is an offset to add to the provisioned metric.

The Reverse TE Metric TLV has Type 20 and Length 4 octets. It has the same two flags, applied to the traffic engineering metric, a 24-bit RESERVED field that MUST be 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt, and a four-octet unsigned Reverse TE Metric.
sections.eli5: The message is a small form: a type number, a size, two tick boxes (only if bigger, and add it on) and the new length of the road.

sections.title: Procedures
sections.content:
A router that receives a Hello with the Reverse Metric TLV MUST use the RM to derive the metric for the link in its Router-LSA, when the RM feature is enabled. How the sender picks the value is implementation specific and outside the scope.

  • If the O flag is set, the advertised metric is the provisioned metric plus the TLV value, capped at 0xffff (maximum interface cost) if the sum is too large.
  • If O is clear, the advertised metric is copied from the TLV.
  • If H is set and O is clear, the value is copied only when it is higher than the provisioned metric.
  • H and O are mutually exclusive, and H is ignored when O is set.

When the sender stops including the TLV, the neighbor MUST revert to its provisioned metric.

To avoid instability when routers signal on the same link, the RFC RECOMMENDS that an RM value a router signals not be derived from RM values signaled by its neighbors. It should use its own provisioned local metrics.

With multi-topology routing, a router MAY include multiple Reverse Metric TLVs, one per MTID, but MUST NOT include more than one per MTID. A receiver uses only the first instance for an MTID. The Reverse TE Metric TLV MAY be used the same way for the TE metric in the Link TLV of the TE Opaque LSA.
sections.eli5: If the neighbor gets a request, it either uses the new length, adds to its own, or only uses it when it is longer. When the requests stop, it goes back to normal.

sections.title: Operational Guidelines and Compatibility
sections.content:
A signaled RM does not alter the metric parameters stored in the receiver's persistent provisioning database. Routers that receive an RM advertisement SHOULD log an event, so administrators can find which node is advertising a different metric. When a link TE metric is raised to the maximum, this SHOULD immediately trigger CSPF recalculation.

As a safeguard against inadvertent use, an implementation MUST NOT signal RM by default and MUST provide configuration to enable signaling on specific links. It MUST NOT accept RM by default and MUST support enabling or disabling acceptance on specific links. For the maintenance use case, operators are RECOMMENDED to enable it only for the duration of the maintenance window.

A router that does not support this specification ignores the two new TLVs, so behavior is the same as before. The RFC concludes there are no backward compatibility issues.
sections.eli5: The sign-posting is off until someone turns it on, and the crew should take the sign down when the work is finished. Routers that do not understand the sign just ignore it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5613 also apply. Since the point of the TLVs is to change the metrics routers use, tampering with them can cause traffic to be misrouted. If authentication is used in the OSPFv2 domain, the Cryptographic Authentication TLV MUST also be used to protect the LLS block.

A misbehaving router that sends varying RM values or toggles RM can force neighbors to update their Router-LSAs often, causing churn. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to detect frequent RM changes and ignore the RM, reverting to provisioned metrics, in that case. Logging of malformed LLS TLVs SHOULD be done but MUST be rate-limited to guard against denial of service.
sections.eli5: Someone faking the sign could send cars the wrong way, so the sign must be protected. If a sign keeps flipping, the neighbor should ignore it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered two code points in the "Link Local Signalling TLV Identifiers (LLS Types)" registry: 19 for the Reverse Metric TLV and 20 for the Reverse TE Metric TLV.
sections.eli5: The two new message types were given official numbers in the shared list, 19 and 20.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the TLV value in octets.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Undefined flag bits; MUST be 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: Value is an offset added to the provisioned metric.

fields.name: H
fields.desc: Use the value only if higher than the provisioned metric.

fields.name: Reverse Metric
fields.desc: Value or offset that replaces or is added to the provisioned metric.

items.label: H
items.desc: Use the value only if it is higher than the provisioned metric.

items.label: O
items.desc: The value is an offset added to the provisioned metric.
